newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Zaire crisis may provide opportunity.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Zaire crisis may provide opportunity.

text.p: The international community plans to set up new relief depots in Rwanda aimed at enticing refugees home and turning the crisis on Zaire's border into an opportunity for improved stability, a senior U.S. official said on Monday.

The official, Administrator Brian Atwood of the Agency for International Development, told reporters the fighting and chaos on Zaire's border with Rwanda and Burundi is "probably the biggest crisis going on in the world today."
He also said it appeared that Rwandan military forces had helped Tutsis in the weekend offensive in eastern Zaire and this is an ominous development in the crisis.

The fighting pits Zairean troops against ethnic Tutsi rebels and has put a question mark over the future integrity of Zaire, whose President Mobutu Sese Seko has spent more than two months in Switzerland for cancer treatment.
The conflict has forced hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees in Zaire on the move.
Zaire was the major topic at Monday's meeting of U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher's senior staff. But officials said Washington has little leverage over the situation.
Atwood and other officials acknowledged that Zaire's disintegration, which experts say looks increasingly likely, would have grave consequences for regional stability.

In such a case, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States would "obviously react" but has not considered what that reaction might be. "We're not actively planning upstairs for this to happen," he said.
Atwood said Washington last week sent a disaster relief team to Rwanda and was working with the World Food Programme and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees.

The goal is "to try to set up what we hope will be magnets -- food and water and relief (centers) -- inside Rwanda," he said. The last international aid workers on Monday left the Zairean town of Bukavu near major refugee camps.

"We are hoping that we can defuse a problem that has existed for a while and encourage people to come back home. The Rwandan government has taken the position that it wants people to come home and wants the United Nations to be feeding people in Rwanda not on the borders. If that's the case then they have an opportunity themselves to make this happen," Atwood said.

For Hutu refugees living in camps in eastern Zaire, a return to Rwanda which they fled two years ago would be a gamble. Many fear reprisals for the genocide of Rwandan Tutsis in 1994 by Hutus. But over the weekend the fighting caused some 3,000 refugees to go back to Rwanda.

So far international efforts to resolve the problem have not succeeded but "we're going to have to look at this challenge as a new opportunity hopefully to get people to go back into Rwanda," Atwood said.
Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu denied giving military help to rebels in eastern Zaire, although he morally backed their fight against "extermination" by Zaire authorites.
Atwood said: "No one identified those who raided (Hutu refugee border camps at the weekend) but it appears that they were Rwanda army forces," aiding Tutsi Banyamulenge forces.
The Banyamulenge, from a 300,000-strong Tutsi community that migrated from what is now Rwanda to Zaire up to 200 years ago, have taken a string of towns south of Bukavu and were heading for Bukavu.

"You've got the possibility here that Tutsis are attempting to create a 'cordon sanitaire' along the border with the Banyamulenge people and Rwandan forces ... This is probably the biggest crisis going on in the world today in terms of numbers of people and movement," Atwood said.
